Data science-driven design is an approach to design that utilizes data science techniques and tools to inform and optimize the design process. The goal is to create designs that are not only aesthetically pleasing but also effective and efficient in meeting user needs and business objectives.

Data science-driven design involves the collection, analysis, and interpretation of data related to user behavior, preferences, and needs. This data is then used to inform design decisions, such as layout, color scheme, typography, and functionality. By analyzing data, designers can gain insights into how users interact with a product, identify areas for improvement, and make data-driven decisions to enhance the user experience.

Examples of data science-driven design in action include A/B testing, user surveys, heat mapping, and user behavior analytics. A/B testing involves testing two versions of a design to see which performs better with users. User surveys and interviews can provide valuable insights into user needs and preferences. Heat mapping can show which parts of a design users are interacting with the most. User behavior analytics can help identify patterns in user behavior and inform design decisions.

properties.name: User Intuition
properties.description:
User Intuition conducts customer research across chat, voice, and video, transforming real customer conversations into continuous, compounding intelligence.

We replace slow, project-based research with natural, dynamic 1:1 conversations that capture how customers actually think, feel, and decide. Instead of relying on panels, surveys, or scripted interviews, we engage real customers in the moments that matter - after a win or loss, during churn, inside a product experience, or while evaluating a new concept.

Every conversation becomes part of a growing intelligence layer. Insights aren’t trapped in slide decks or lost after a study ends. They are structured, searchable, and reusable, so teams can query past research, connect themes across time, and answer new questions without starting from scratch.

Our platform works across chat, voice, and video, adapting to the context while maintaining research rigor. Behind the scenes, customer narratives are translated into structured insight: emotions, triggers, jobs-to-be-done, competitive references, and supporting evidence. This turns qualitative feedback into something teams can analyze, compare, and build on over time.

The result is customer intelligence that compounds. Each study strengthens the system, lowers the cost of future insights, and increases confidence in the decisions that matter most.

User Intuition is built for teams that need speed, depth, and trust in their customer understanding and want research that gets more valuable every time it’s used.

entity.name: CrowAI.co
entity.description:
CrowAI is an AI-native experimentation engine for conversion optimization and A/B testing that replaces $50K–$400K CRO tools and teams with fully automated experiments in minutes. It enables teams to run significantly more experiments and unlock compounding revenue growth through continuous optimization.

Most teams don’t have a testing problem, they have an execution problem. Ideas sit in backlogs, experiments take weeks to launch, and opportunities are often lost before they are tested.

CrowAI addresses this by rethinking experimentation from the ground up. Instead of relying on fragmented workflows across research, design, development, and QA, the entire process runs within a single automated system, from insight to deployment.

Experimentation has long depended on manual workflows and cross-team coordination. CrowAI replaces this with an AI-native system where experiments are generated, built, and deployed autonomously. From identifying funnel leaks and generating hypotheses to producing variant code, configuring tests, and rolling out winning experiences, the platform handles the full lifecycle.

This shift fundamentally changes how teams operate. By removing execution bottlenecks, teams can run 10× more experiments and translate every insight into action within minutes instead of weeks. The result is a continuous optimization loop that drives faster learning, better decisions, and measurable revenue impact.

CrowAI is built for growth and marketing teams focused on conversion and ROAS, product teams looking to ship and validate ideas faster, and engineering teams aiming to reduce experimentation-related workload.

Trusted by 50+ partners across e-commerce, BFSI, retail, and SaaS, CrowAI is built with enterprise-grade security standards, including ISO 27001, GDPR, CCPA, and SOC 2 Type II, with a privacy-first architecture.

Turn your experimentation into a continuous growth engine.
Learn more at https://www.crowai.co

entity.name: Parcha.io
entity.description:
Data science-driven design is an approach to design that utilizes data science techniques and tools to inform and optimize the design process. The goal is to create designs that are not only aesthetically pleasing but also effective and efficient in meeting user needs and business objectives.

Data science-driven design involves the collection, analysis, and interpretation of data related to user behavior, preferences, and needs. This data is then used to inform design decisions, such as layout, color scheme, typography, and functionality. By analyzing data, designers can gain insights into how users interact with a product, identify areas for improvement, and make data-driven decisions to enhance the user experience.

Examples of data science-driven design in action include A/B testing, user surveys, heat mapping, and user behavior analytics. A/B testing involves testing two versions of a design to see which performs better with users. User surveys and interviews can provide valuable insights into user needs and preferences. Heat mapping can show which parts of a design users are interacting with the most. User behavior analytics can help identify patterns in user behavior and inform design decisions.

messages.content:
You are an evaluator scoring company lookalike results for a B2B benchmark.

Definition - a company lookalike API takes a seed company and returns other
companies that resemble it. Resemblance has two halves, and they are judged
DIFFERENTLY:

  ANCHOR       - who the seed sells to, and what it fundamentally is
                 (e.g. "restaurant point-of-sale platform"). This is a HARD
                 requirement. Every lookalike must be the same kind of company
                 for the same kind of customer. No amount of feature overlap
                 substitutes for it.
  CAPABILITIES - what the seed does (e.g. payments, online ordering, payroll,
                 operations). A lookalike matches ANY non-empty subset. It does
                 not need all of them, and matching more is not required to
                 qualify - only to be a closer match.

So: a true lookalike clears the ANCHOR and shares at least one CAPABILITY.

You will be given:
  • A SEED company - the company the lookalike search started from, with its
    ANCHOR and its CAPABILITIES listed separately.
  • A CANDIDATE company - a lookalike returned by a vendor's API.

Decide in this order, and do not work backwards from a conclusion:

STEP 1 - anchor_match (the gate).
  True only if the CANDIDATE is the same kind of company as the ANCHOR, for
  the same kind of customer. Ask: would someone shopping for the SEED consider
  this company to be in the same market?
    - A different customer fails, even in the same product category
      (restaurant POS vs retail-only POS: the customer differs).
    - A different category fails, even for the same customer
      (a restaurant POS vs a restaurant-supply distributor: both sell to
      restaurants, but only one is the same kind of company).
    - Serving the category rather than competing in it fails: agencies,
      consultancies, integrators, resellers.
    - Being a customer of the category fails (an actual restaurant is not a
      lookalike of a restaurant POS platform).
    - Parent/holding companies, the seed itself, and duplicate or parody
      entries fail.
  When you cannot tell what the candidate sells, anchor_match is false.

STEP 2 - capabilities_matched (the overlap).
  List the SEED capabilities this candidate also does, copying the strings
  verbatim from the SEED's list. Include a capability when the candidate
  plausibly offers it as part of its product; leave it out when you have no
  evidence. Matching a subset is normal and expected.

STEP 3 - relevant.
  relevant = anchor_match AND capabilities_matched is non-empty.
  Nothing else changes it.

Rules that apply throughout:
  - Do NOT require comparable company size, headcount, revenue, funding,
    geography, maturity, or platform breadth. A smaller, larger, or
    differently-located company clears the anchor if it is the same kind of
    company for the same kind of customer. Ignore such metadata.
  - A shared generic taxonomy label or keyword is not an anchor match. Neither
    is a similar technology stack - tech co-signals may support a judgement but
    never establish one.
  - Judge the candidate's primary business, not a side feature.
  - When in doubt on the anchor, answer false.
  - Keep the rationale ≤ 25 words: name the anchor verdict and the overlap.

Worked examples (SEED anchor -> candidate -> verdict):
  - "restaurant point-of-sale platform" [payments, online ordering, payroll]
      • a restaurant POS suite with payments and online ordering
        -> anchor true, matched [payments, online ordering], relevant true.
      • a restaurant POS with none of the listed capabilities
        -> anchor true, matched [], relevant FALSE (no overlap).
      • a retail-only POS with payments
        -> anchor FALSE (different customer), relevant false.
      • a general payments processor with no restaurant POS product
        -> anchor FALSE (different category), relevant false.
      • an actual restaurant chain
        -> anchor FALSE (customer of the category), relevant false.
      • an agency that installs restaurant POS systems
        -> anchor FALSE (serves the category), relevant false.
  - "CRM and marketing automation platform for go-to-market teams"
      • a smaller CRM with marketing automation -> anchor true, relevant true.
      • a lead-generation agency using that CRM for clients -> anchor false.
  - "digital bank for consumers"
      • a digital bank in another country -> anchor true (geography is not a
        constraint), relevant true if any capability overlaps.
  - "developer-security platform"
      • a company on a similar cloud stack selling HR software -> anchor false.

Definition - a company lookalike API takes a seed company and returns other
companies that resemble it. Resemblance has two halves, and they are judged
DIFFERENTLY:

  ANCHOR       - who the seed sells to, and what it fundamentally is
                 (e.g. "restaurant point-of-sale platform"). This is a HARD
                 requirement. Every lookalike must be the same kind of company
                 for the same kind of customer. No amount of feature overlap
                 substitutes for it.
  CAPABILITIES - what the seed does (e.g. payments, online ordering, payroll,
                 operations). A lookalike matches ANY non-empty subset. It does
                 not need all of them, and matching more is not required to
                 qualify - only to be a closer match.

So: a true lookalike clears the ANCHOR and shares at least one CAPABILITY.

You will be given:
  • A SEED company - the company the lookalike search started from, with its
    ANCHOR and its CAPABILITIES listed separately.
  • A CANDIDATE company - a lookalike returned by a vendor's API.

Decide in this order, and do not work backwards from a conclusion:

STEP 1 - anchor_match (the gate).
  True only if the CANDIDATE is the same kind of company as the ANCHOR, for
  the same kind of customer. Ask: would someone shopping for the SEED consider
  this company to be in the same market?
    - A different customer fails, even in the same product category
      (restaurant POS vs retail-only POS: the customer differs).
    - A different category fails, even for the same customer
      (a restaurant POS vs a restaurant-supply distributor: both sell to
      restaurants, but only one is the same kind of company).
    - Serving the category rather than competing in it fails: agencies,
      consultancies, integrators, resellers.

      lookalike of a restaurant POS platform).

      entries fail.

  plausibly offers it as part of its product; leave it out when you have no
  evidence. Matching a subset is normal and expected.

    is a similar technology stack - tech co-signals may support a judgement but
    never establish one.
  - Judge the candidate's primary business, not a side feature.
  - When in doubt on the anchor, answer false.
  - Keep the rationale ≤ 25 words: name the anchor verdict and the overlap.

You are an evaluator scoring company lookalike results for a B2B benchmark.

Definition - a company lookalike API takes a seed company and returns other
companies that resemble it. Resemblance has two halves, and they are judged
DIFFERENTLY:

  ANCHOR       - who the seed sells to, and what it fundamentally is
                 (e.g. "restaurant point-of-sale platform"). This is a HARD
                 requirement. Every lookalike must be the same kind of company
                 for the same kind of customer. No amount of feature overlap
                 substitutes for it.
  CAPABILITIES - what the seed does (e.g. payments, online ordering, payroll,
                 operations). A lookalike matches ANY non-empty subset. It does
                 not need all of them, and matching more is not required to
                 qualify - only to be a closer match.

So: a true lookalike clears the ANCHOR and shares at least one CAPABILITY.

You will be given:
  • A SEED company - the company the lookalike search started from, with its
    ANCHOR and its CAPABILITIES listed separately.
  • A CANDIDATE company - a lookalike returned by a vendor's API.

Decide in this order, and do not work backwards from a conclusion:

STEP 1 - anchor_match (the gate).
  True only if the CANDIDATE is the same kind of company as the ANCHOR, for
  the same kind of customer. Ask: would someone shopping for the SEED consider
  this company to be in the same market?
    - A different customer fails, even in the same product category
      (restaurant POS vs retail-only POS: the customer differs).
    - A different category fails, even for the same customer
      (a restaurant POS vs a restaurant-supply distributor: both sell to
      restaurants, but only one is the same kind of company).
    - Serving the category rather than competing in it fails: agencies,
      consultancies, integrators, resellers.
    - Being a customer of the category fails (an actual restaurant is not a
      lookalike of a restaurant POS platform).
    - Parent/holding companies, the seed itself, and duplicate or parody
      entries fail.
  When you cannot tell what the candidate sells, anchor_match is false.

STEP 2 - capabilities_matched (the overlap).

  verbatim from the SEED's list. Include a capability when the candidate
  plausibly offers it as part of its product; leave it out when you have no
  evidence. Matching a subset is normal and expected.

  relevant = anchor_match AND capabilities_matched is non-empty.
  Nothing else changes it.

    geography, maturity, or platform breadth. A smaller, larger, or
    differently-located company clears the anchor if it is the same kind of
    company for the same kind of customer. Ignore such metadata.
  - A shared generic taxonomy label or keyword is not an anchor match. Neither
    is a similar technology stack - tech co-signals may support a judgement but
    never establish one.
  - Judge the candidate's primary business, not a side feature.
  - When in doubt on the anchor, answer false.
  - Keep the rationale ≤ 25 words: name the anchor verdict and the overlap.

        -> anchor FALSE (different category), relevant false.
      • an actual restaurant chain
        -> anchor FALSE (customer of the category), relevant false.

        -> anchor FALSE (serves the category), relevant false.
  - "CRM and marketing automation platform for go-to-market teams"
      • a smaller CRM with marketing automation -> anchor true, relevant true.

    - A different customer fails, even in the same product category

Definition - a company lookalike API takes a seed company and returns other
companies that resemble it. Resemblance has two halves, and they are judged
DIFFERENTLY:

  ANCHOR       - who the seed sells to, and what it fundamentally is
                 (e.g. "restaurant point-of-sale platform"). This is a HARD
                 requirement. Every lookalike must be the same kind of company
                 for the same kind of customer. No amount of feature overlap
                 substitutes for it.
  CAPABILITIES - what the seed does (e.g. payments, online ordering, payroll,
                 operations). A lookalike matches ANY non-empty subset. It does
                 not need all of them, and matching more is not required to
                 qualify - only to be a closer match.

So: a true lookalike clears the ANCHOR and shares at least one CAPABILITY.

You will be given:
  • A SEED company - the company the lookalike search started from, with its
    ANCHOR and its CAPABILITIES listed separately.
  • A CANDIDATE company - a lookalike returned by a vendor's API.

Decide in this order, and do not work backwards from a conclusion:

STEP 1 - anchor_match (the gate).
  True only if the CANDIDATE is the same kind of company as the ANCHOR, for
  the same kind of customer. Ask: would someone shopping for the SEED consider
  this company to be in the same market?
    - A different customer fails, even in the same product category
      (restaurant POS vs retail-only POS: the customer differs).
    - A different category fails, even for the same customer
      (a restaurant POS vs a restaurant-supply distributor: both sell to
      restaurants, but only one is the same kind of company).
    - Serving the category rather than competing in it fails: agencies,
      consultancies, integrators, resellers.
    - Being a customer of the category fails (an actual restaurant is not a
      lookalike of a restaurant POS platform).
    - Parent/holding companies, the seed itself, and duplicate or parody
      entries fail.
  When you cannot tell what the candidate sells, anchor_match is false.

STEP 2 - capabilities_matched (the overlap).
  List the SEED capabilities this candidate also does, copying the strings
  verbatim from the SEED's list. Include a capability when the candidate
  plausibly offers it as part of its product; leave it out when you have no
  evidence. Matching a subset is normal and expected.

  Nothing else changes it.

      • a smaller CRM with marketing automation -> anchor true, relevant true.

Definition - a company lookalike API takes a seed company and returns other
companies that resemble it. Resemblance has two halves, and they are judged
DIFFERENTLY:

  ANCHOR       - who the seed sells to, and what it fundamentally is
                 (e.g. "restaurant point-of-sale platform"). This is a HARD
                 requirement. Every lookalike must be the same kind of company
                 for the same kind of customer. No amount of feature overlap
                 substitutes for it.
  CAPABILITIES - what the seed does (e.g. payments, online ordering, payroll,
                 operations). A lookalike matches ANY non-empty subset. It does
                 not need all of them, and matching more is not required to
                 qualify - only to be a closer match.

So: a true lookalike clears the ANCHOR and shares at least one CAPABILITY.

You will be given:
  • A SEED company - the company the lookalike search started from, with its
    ANCHOR and its CAPABILITIES listed separately.
  • A CANDIDATE company - a lookalike returned by a vendor's API.

Decide in this order, and do not work backwards from a conclusion:

STEP 1 - anchor_match (the gate).
  True only if the CANDIDATE is the same kind of company as the ANCHOR, for
  the same kind of customer. Ask: would someone shopping for the SEED consider
  this company to be in the same market?
    - A different customer fails, even in the same product category
      (restaurant POS vs retail-only POS: the customer differs).
    - A different category fails, even for the same customer
      (a restaurant POS vs a restaurant-supply distributor: both sell to
      restaurants, but only one is the same kind of company).
    - Serving the category rather than competing in it fails: agencies,
      consultancies, integrators, resellers.
    - Being a customer of the category fails (an actual restaurant is not a
      lookalike of a restaurant POS platform).
    - Parent/holding companies, the seed itself, and duplicate or parody
      entries fail.
  When you cannot tell what the candidate sells, anchor_match is false.

STEP 2 - capabilities_matched (the overlap).
  List the SEED capabilities this candidate also does, copying the strings
  verbatim from the SEED's list. Include a capability when the candidate
  plausibly offers it as part of its product; leave it out when you have no
  evidence. Matching a subset is normal and expected.

STEP 3 - relevant.
  relevant = anchor_match AND capabilities_matched is non-empty.
  Nothing else changes it.

Rules that apply throughout:
  - Do NOT require comparable company size, headcount, revenue, funding,
    geography, maturity, or platform breadth. A smaller, larger, or
    differently-located company clears the anchor if it is the same kind of
    company for the same kind of customer. Ignore such metadata.
  - A shared generic taxonomy label or keyword is not an anchor match. Neither
    is a similar technology stack - tech co-signals may support a judgement but
    never establish one.
  - Judge the candidate's primary business, not a side feature.
  - When in doubt on the anchor, answer false.
  - Keep the rationale ≤ 25 words: name the anchor verdict and the overlap.

Worked examples (SEED anchor -> candidate -> verdict):
  - "restaurant point-of-sale platform" [payments, online ordering, payroll]
      • a restaurant POS suite with payments and online ordering
        -> anchor true, matched [payments, online ordering], relevant true.
      • a restaurant POS with none of the listed capabilities
        -> anchor true, matched [], relevant FALSE (no overlap).
      • a retail-only POS with payments
        -> anchor FALSE (different customer), relevant false.
      • a general payments processor with no restaurant POS product
        -> anchor FALSE (different category), relevant false.
      • an actual restaurant chain
        -> anchor FALSE (customer of the category), relevant false.
      • an agency that installs restaurant POS systems
        -> anchor FALSE (serves the category), relevant false.
  - "CRM and marketing automation platform for go-to-market teams"
      • a smaller CRM with marketing automation -> anchor true, relevant true.
      • a lead-generation agency using that CRM for clients -> anchor false.
  - "digital bank for consumers"
      • a digital bank in another country -> anchor true (geography is not a
        constraint), relevant true if any capability overlaps.
  - "developer-security platform"
      • a company on a similar cloud stack selling HR software -> anchor false.

SEED:
  name: Amplitude
  domain: amplitude.com
  ANCHOR (hard requirement): product analytics platform
  CAPABILITIES (match any subset):
    - user behavior analysis
    - experimentation
    - digital-product growth

CANDIDATE:
  name: Metriken
  description: Automatically collects, analyses product data, and eliminates complexities. Privacy-first by design.
  extras: {"url": "https://linkedin.com/company/metrikenai", "entity": {"name": "Metriken", "foundedYear": 2023, "description": "Automatically collects, analyses product data, and eliminates complexities. Privacy-first by design.", "workforce": null, "headquarters": {"address": "Munich, Bavaria, DE", "city": "Munich", "postalCode": null, "country": "Germany"}, "financials": null, "webTraffic": null, "research": null}}

judge_calls.raw_response: {"anchor_match":true,"capabilities_matched":["user behavior analysis","digital-product growth"],"relevant":true,"rationale":"Product analytics platform collecting and analyzing product data; overlaps user behavior analysis and product growth insights."}

parsed_response.rationale: Product analytics platform collecting and analyzing product data; overlaps user behavior analysis and product growth insights.
